Flood Insurance Data

Buying a house in a flood zone

Across the U.S., NFIP policies on single-family primary homes first bought in the past year cost a median of $1,011 a year, premium plus fees (187,522 policies). Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside those zones, a lender may still require it.

Such single-family primary-home policies

FEMA OpenFEMA NFIP Policies v3, as of August 31, 2026. The figure is the median premium plus fees on single-family primary-home policies first written in the 12 months to that date. It is not a quote: a new policy is priced for the building.

What the lender can require

How much. Where a federally regulated lender must require it, the legal minimum is the loan balance or the NFIP's limit for the property, whichever is less (42 U.S.C. §4012a(b)).

If you do not buy it. If such a lender notifies you that coverage is needed and you do not buy it within 45 days, the lender must buy it for you and can charge you for it (42 U.S.C. §4012a(e)).

A private policy instead. Federal law tells federal lending regulators to direct regulated lending institutions "to accept private flood insurance as satisfaction of the flood insurance coverage requirement" when the private policy's coverage "meets the requirements for coverage" under that requirement (42 U.S.C. §4012a(b)(1)(B)). A private policy's price is not in FEMA's records.

When the policy starts

Most NFIP policies take effect 30 days after you buy, so a policy bought today will not cover a flood this week.

Bought while taking out, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, coverage can start at the loan closing. The insurer must get the form and full amount due within 10 calendar days of closing, or within 30 if your lender, title company or settlement attorney pays. Contents-only coverage qualifies only if the contents are part of the security for the loan.

The seller's policy. Buying a finished home with an NFIP building policy: the seller can assign the policy to you in writing when title transfers.

If you think the zone is wrong

If you think a lender's high-risk-zone finding is wrong, you and the lender together can ask FEMA to review it within 45 days of the lender's notice; a fee applies (44 CFR §65.17).

Our flood zone lookup shows the zone FEMA's map gives an address.

What this page cannot tell you

This house's premium, its flood zone (only FEMA's map and the lender's determination can say), whether a seller's policy can be assigned to you, or private insurers' prices.
